record.paper_title: Towards Event-Triggered NMPC for Efficient 6G Communications: Experimental Results and Open Problems
record.context_brief: Experimental generalization across applications and networks
record.original_question: How well do event-triggered nonlinear model predictive control methods for networked control systems generalize beyond a Furuta pendulum controlled over a tailored O-RAN 6G research platform? The open validation problem is to run further experiments across diverse control applications and communication systems, rather than relying only on numerical simulations or a small number of hardware demonstrations, and to determine whether the control-performance and communication-resource benefits persist in those settings.

evidence.quote: Despite an extensive theoretical analysis of event-triggered MPC and event-triggered control more broadly, most papers illustrate the proposed schemes via numerical simulations only.

As highlighted in [14], experimental studies are crucial for advancing research in NCS. They provide valuable insights into control performance and communication resource requirements for control applications in both current and future wireless networks.
Only a limited number of works explore real hardware implementations: [16], [17] implement their applications using wired experimental setups.

In this paper, we investigate the potential for co-design of model predictive control and network communication. To this end, we design and implement an event-triggered nonlinear model predictive controller for stabilizing a Furuta pendulum communicating over a tailored open radio access network 6G research platform.
Finally, further experiments with diverse control applications and communication systems are needed to advance networked control applications.

artifact.category_tag: event-triggered nonlinear MPC over wireless networks
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a networked control system (NCS) in which a plant with nonlinear continuous-time dynamics x'(t)=f(x(t),u(t)), x(t)∈R^n, u(t)∈U⊂R^m, is stabilized by a nonlinear model predictive controller (NMPC) that, at sampling instants t_k, solves the finite-horizon optimal control problem min ∫_{t_k}^{t_k+T} ℓ(x(τ),u(τ))dτ + V_f(x(t_k+T)) subject to the dynamics, x(t_k)=x_meas, u(τ)∈U and x(τ)∈X, and applies the resulting optimal input until the next sampling instant. Suppose furthermore that the controller and plant communicate over a (possibly wireless) digital network and that an event-triggering rule is used: a new measurement is transmitted, and/or a new optimization is performed, only when a triggering condition g(x(t), x̂(t)) ≥ 0 holds, where x̂(t) is a predicted state used in lieu of fresh data; otherwise no transmission occurs. Such an event-triggered NMPC scheme is parameterised by a triggering threshold and prediction model, and is intended to (i) preserve closed-loop stability and constraint satisfaction and (ii) reduce the average rate of network communications compared with periodic NMPC.

Problem. Empirically and quantitatively characterise the generalisation of event-triggered NMPC schemes for NCS across a broad family of control plants {f_i} (e.g. underactuated mechanical systems, vehicular and robotic platforms, process-control benchmarks) and across a broad family of communication systems {N_j} (e.g. different wireless standards, latency/jitter/loss profiles, scheduling policies and physical-layer parameters). Specifically: design and execute physical hardware experiments across multiple plant–network pairs (f_i, N_j) and determine whether the claimed closed-loop control-performance metrics (e.g. settling time, tracking error, constraint violation rates) and communication-resource metrics (e.g. average transmission rate, channel occupancy, energy per useful transmission) continue to hold, and identify conditions on (f_i, N_j) under which these benefits persist or fail.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is an empirical/validation open problem rather than a closed mathematical conjecture; it asks for broad experimental generalisation across plants and wireless networks. No comprehensive cross-platform experimental validation appears in the recent literature; works continue to rely mostly on simulations or single-testbed demonstrations. Status is treated as open.
